title: Sleeping Beauty — Why You Feel It, And Who Decided
description:
The honest version of Sleeping Beauty starts by giving up the comforting part. A good fairy, knowing the princess would be frightened if alone when she wakes, uses her wand to put every living person and animal in the palace and forest asleep, to awaken when the princess does. This was later adapted in French by Charles Perrault in Histoires ou contes du temps passé in 1697.

Every serious account of Sleeping Beauty eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. One day, the new King must go to war against his neighbor, Emperor Contalabutte, and leaves his mother to govern the kingdom and look after his family. After her son leaves, the Ogress Queen Mother sends her daughter-in-law to a house secluded in the woods and orders her cook to prepare Morning with Sauce Robert for dinner.

scenes.narration: The honest version of Sleeping Beauty starts by giving up the comforting part. A good fairy, knowing the princess would be frightened if alone when she wakes, uses her wand to put every living person and animal in the palace and forest asleep, to awaken when the princess does. This was later adapted in French by Charles Perrault in Histoires ou contes du temps passé in 1697.

Strip Sleeping Beauty of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The version collected and printed by the Brothers Grimm was one orally transmitted from the Perrault version, while including its own attributes like the thorny rose hedge and the curse. The Aarne-Thompson classification system for fairy tales lists "Sleeping Beauty" as a Type 410: it includes a princess who is magically forced into sleep and later woken, reversing the magic.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Sleeping Beauty shows exactly where that breaks. The fairy tale has been adapted countless times throughout history and retold by modern storytellers across various media. Early contributions to the tale include the medieval courtly romance Perceforest (c. 1337–1344).

What looks like free choice in Sleeping Beauty is older than choice itself. In this tale, a princess named Zellandine falls in love with a man named Troylus. Her father sends him to perform tasks to prove himself worthy of her, and while he is gone, Zellandine falls into an enchanted sleep.

Nobody designed the part of Sleeping Beauty you experience — it was inherited. When their child is born, the child draws from her finger the flax that caused her sleep. She realizes from the ring Troylus left her that he was the father, and Troylus later returns to marry her.

Every serious account of Sleeping Beauty eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Another early literary predecessor is the Provençal versified novel Fraire de Joi e sor de Plaser (c. 1320–1340). The second part of the Sleeping Beauty tale, in which the princess and her children are almost put to death but instead are hidden, may have been influenced by Genevieve of Brabant.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Sleeping Beauty — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Even earlier influences come from the story of the sleeping Brynhild in the Volsunga saga and the tribulations of saintly female martyrs in early Christian hagiography conventions. Following these early renditions, the tale was first published by Italian poet Giambattista Basile who lived from 1575 to 1632.

The selfish-gene reading of Sleeping Beauty makes it less romantic and far more precise. The folktale begins with a princess whose parents are told by a wicked fairy that their daughter will die when she pricks her finger on a particular item. In Basile's version, the princess pricks her finger on a piece of flax.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. In Perrault's and the Grimm Brothers' versions, the item is a spindle. The parents rid the kingdom of these items in the hopes of protecting their daughter, but the prophecy is fulfilled regardless.

The feeling that Sleeping Beauty means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Instead of dying, as was foretold, the princess falls into a deep sleep. After some time, she is found by a prince and is awakened.

Nothing in Sleeping Beauty was built for you — it was built for reproduction. In Giambattista Basile's version of Sleeping Beauty, Sun, Moon, and Talia, the sleeping beauty, Talia, falls into a deep sleep after getting a splinter of flax in her finger. According to Maria Tatar, there are versions of the story that include a second part to the narrative that details the couple's troubles after their union; some folklorists believe the two parts were originally separate tales.

The psychology underneath Sleeping Beauty is simpler and older than the story on top. The second part begins after the prince and princess have had children. Through the course of the tale, the princess and her children are introduced in some way to another woman from the prince's life.

Behind Sleeping Beauty sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. This other woman is not fond of the prince's new family, and calls a cook to kill the children and serve them for dinner. Before this can happen, the other woman's true nature is revealed to the prince and then she is subjected to the very death that she had planned for the princess.

The nihilist does not deny Sleeping Beauty — he only refuses to flatter it. In Giambattista Basile's dark version of Sleeping Beauty, Sun, Moon, and Talia, the sleeping beauty is named Talia. By asking wise men and astrologers to predict her future after her birth, her father, who is a great Lord, learns that Talia will be in danger from a splinter of flax.

What culture calls destiny in Sleeping Beauty is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Intrigued by the sight of the twirling spindle, Talia invites the woman over and takes the distaff from her hand to stretch the flax. Tragically, the splinter of flax gets embedded under her nail, and she is put to sleep.

The genes do not care about Sleeping Beauty; they care about copies. After Talia falls asleep, she is seated on a velvet throne and her father, to forget his misery of what he thinks is her death, closes the doors and abandons the house forever. One day, while a king is walking by, one of his falcons flies into the house.

Take away the meaning and Sleeping Beauty still functions — that is the disturbing part. The king knocks, hoping to be let in by someone, but no one answers, and he decides to climb in with a ladder. Afterwards, he leaves her in bed and goes back to his kingdom.

The unconscious does not argue with Sleeping Beauty; it simply acts first. Though Talia is unconscious, she gives birth to twins—one of whom keeps sucking her finger. Talia awakens because the twin has sucked the flax from her finger.

Sleeping Beauty feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. When she wakes up, she discovers that she is a mother and has no idea what happened to her. After a few days, the king must return to his realm but promises he'll return to take her to his kingdom.

The bleak reading of Sleeping Beauty is also the most testable one. Back in his kingdom, his wife hears him saying "Talia, Sun, and Moon" in his sleep. She then pretends she is the king and writes to Talia asking her to send the twins.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Sleeping Beauty. On their arrival, the queen orders the cook to kill the twins and make dishes out of them to feed the king; instead, the cook takes the twins to his wife and hides them. Every time the king mentions how good the food is, the queen replies, "Eat, eat, you are eating of your own." Later, the queen invites Talia to the kingdom intending to burn her alive, but the king discovers the truth.

The self that experiences Sleeping Beauty is a committee, not a king. He then orders that his wife be burned along with those who betrayed him, while he rewards the cook. The story ends with the king marrying Talia and living happily ever after.

Reproduction explains more of Sleeping Beauty than any philosophy dares to admit. Perrault's narrative is written in two parts, which some folklorists believe were originally separate tales, as they were in the Brothers Grimm's version, and were later joined by Giambattista Basile and once more by Perrault. According to folklore editors Martin Hallett and Barbara Karasek, Perrault's tale is a much more subtle and pared down version than Basile's story in terms of the more immoral details.

Once you see Sleeping Beauty as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. An example of this is depicted in Perrault's tale by the prince's choice to instigate no physical interaction with the sleeping princess when he discovers her. At the christening of the king and queen's long-awaited child, seven good fairies are invited to be the baby princess's godmothers and bless her.

The story Sleeping Beauty tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. At the palace banquet, each fairy receives a golden box of bejeweled utensils. Then, an old fairy arrives, forgotten because she has not left her tower in fifty years and was thought to be dead.

Meaning is not found in Sleeping Beauty — it is manufactured for it. Nevertheless, she is given a seat and a box of plain utensils. When the seventh fairy hears her muttering threats, she hides behind the curtains, determined to give her gift last in case the uninvited guest tries to harm the princess.

The cold light on Sleeping Beauty leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. After the first six fairies have bestowed their gifts on the princess, the eighth fairy, furious at not being invited, curses the princess so that one day she will prick her finger on a spindle and die. The seventh fairy then offers her gift, attempting to soften the curse by having the princess fall into a deep sleep for a century, to be awakened by a prince.

Sleeping Beauty did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The King then orders all spinning wheels in the kingdom banned and destroyed in an attempt to avert the eighth fairy's curse on his daughter. One day, after the Princess has come of age, She wanders through the palace rooms and comes across an old woman—really the evil fairy in disguise—spinning at her wheel.

The honest version of Sleeping Beauty starts by giving up the comforting part. The Princess, having never seen one before, asks to try it, but as soon as she pricks her finger on the spindle, the curse is fulfilled and she falls into a deep sleep. The old woman cries for help, and efforts to revive the Princess fail.

Strip Sleeping Beauty of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The seventh fairy, foreseeing the Princess's distress upon waking alone, casts a spell to put everyone in the castle to sleep, except the King and Queen. After kissing their daughter goodbye, they leave to prevent anyone from disturbing her, while the fairy summons a forest to grow around the castle, hiding it from the world.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Sleeping Beauty shows exactly where that breaks. After a hundred years, a prince from another royal family comes across a hidden castle during a hunting trip. An old man shares its history, telling him that a king's son is destined to awaken the princess.

What looks like free choice in Sleeping Beauty is older than choice itself. The prince pushes through the forest, enters the castle, and is captivated by her unmatched beauty. The spell breaks, the princess wakes, and she gives the prince a look "more tender than a first glance might seem to warrant" (in Perrault's original French tale, there is no kiss).

Nobody designed the part of Sleeping Beauty you experience — it was inherited. Eventually, the prince and princess are married in the castle chapel by the chaplain. After marrying the Sleeping Beauty in secret, the Prince visits her for four years and she bears him two children, unbeknownst to his mother, who is an ogre.

Every serious account of Sleeping Beauty eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. One day, the new King must go to war against his neighbor, Emperor Contalabutte, and leaves his mother to govern the kingdom and look after his family.
